item.title: Strengthening Democratic Values and Alliances: Stiftung Mercator Funded 80 New Projects in 2025
item.description:
Last year, the Ruhr-based charitable organisation supported a further 80 projects with funding totalling approximately €61.3 million. At the same time, it further developed the strategies of its four centres: Digital Society, Europe in the World, Climate-Resilient Society, and Participation and Cohesion. These developments are outlined in the 2025 Annual Report, published today. 

At a time of growing social polarisation and political upheaval, civil society organisations engaged in public and political life are facing increasing pressure. “This challenges us to learn even more consistently across programme areas and to continuously adapt our approaches,” said Dr Lars Grotewold, who assumed the role of Chief Executive Officer at the beginning of the year. “With this in mind, we have refined our strategy for the next five years, guided by the ambition expressed in our motto: #StandingUpForDemocracy

Climate adaptation, platforms for protected dialogue 

The organisation’s former Centre for Climate Action has evolved its strategic approach to combine socially balanced climate policy and emissions reduction with adaptation to the impacts of climate change. 

The Centre for Digital Society promotes the responsible use of digital technologies in line with democratic values – and, for example, is striving to limit the market power of a small number of large corporations through competition policy. 

As international cooperation faces mounting geopolitical challenges, the Centre for Europe in the World has intensified systematic cross-border exchange with partners across Africa, Asia and Latin America and established platforms for protected dialogue. Meanwhile, the Centre for Participation and Cohesion is placing an even stronger emphasis on improving participation for socio-economically disadvantaged communities and strengthening democratic institutions, particularly at the local level. At the same time, the organisation continued to expand its community-building activities as a strategic priority. 

Since its establishment in 1996, the organisation has supported 2,240 projects with total funding of approximately €1.08 billion (as of the end of 2025). The funding is available to universities and research institutions, civil society organisations and think tanks, with most grants awarded over several years.

ABOUT STIFTUNG MERCATOR 

Stiftung Mercator is a private, independent and charitable organisation that bases its work on scientific expertise and practical project experience. Since 1996, it has been committed to fostering a more inclusive, participatory and cohesive society. To achieve this, it develops and supports projects that improve opportunities for participation and strengthen social cohesion. 

The organisation is committed to a democratic and effective Europe, a digital transformation of the state and society rooted in fundamental rights, and a resilient, socially balanced climate policy. These goals can only be realised within a liberal democracy, which Stiftung Mercator is committed to protecting and strengthening – as reflected in its motto: #StandingupforDemocracy. 

Stiftung Mercator works in Germany, across Europe and internationally. It also maintains a special commitment to the Ruhr region, the home of the founding family and the organisation’s headquarters.

item.title: Stiftung Mercator: New Leadership for the Europe in the World Centre
item.description:
Dr Magdalena Kirchner, Director of the Europe in the World Centre at Stiftung Mercator, has decided to pursue a new professional direction for personal reasons. Dr Christian Straube, previously a project manager in the centre, has taken over her responsibilities on an interim basis. 

“Working in a challenging international environment, Magdalena Kirchner has played a key role in further developing the strategic direction of our Europe in the World programme portfolio. Her achievements include strengthening multilateral approaches to addressing global challenges, shaping and expanding our partnerships across Europe, and enhancing the resilience of European democracies and societies,” says Dr Lars Grotewold, Chief Executive Officer of Stiftung Mercator. “We are sincerely grateful for her dedication and contributions and wish her every success in the future.” 

Dr Kirchner’s departure is taking place on the best of terms and at her own request. She has headed the Europe in the World Centre since 1 January 2024 and will leave the organization at the end of her parental leave in April 2027. 

Dr Christian Straube, who holds a doctorate in Ethnology and Sinology, has been with Stiftung Mercator since 1 November 2022. He will lead the division on an interim basis until a successor has been appointed.

item.title: Strengthening democracy in everyday life: Stiftung Mercator supports nationwide “Ehrentag”
item.description:
To mark the anniversary of Germany’s Basic Law on 23 May, Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has launched a new initiative called “Ehrentag”. Stiftung Mercator is one of the partners supporting the initiative, which aims to recognise and honour voluntary civic engagement – as democracy depends on people who contribute to the common good, take responsibility, and foster social cohesion.

At a time of rapid political and economic change, initiatives, associations, neighbourhood networks and civil society organisations help counteract centrifugal forces within society. Wherever people come together and engage constructively with differences, they experience a sense of agency and belonging.

“Democracy means much more than elections or institutions. It is rooted in civic engagement, taking responsibility, and a willingness to find solutions together. The Federal President’s “Ehrentag” highlights how strongly our democracy is sustained by many – especially by an organised and politically active civil society,” says Dr Lars Grotewold, Chief Executive Officer of Stiftung Mercator.

An important signal for society

Stiftung Mercator is committed to a cohesive, open, and socially just society, to the rule of law and equal opportunities, and to safeguarding our natural resources. Under the motto #WeStrengthenDemocracy, the organisation supports projects and partnerships that promote participation, strengthen social cohesion and foster constructive public debate, among other goals.

The nationwide initiative “Ehrentag” sends a strong signal, underscoring that democracy must be continually re-explained, re-lived, and re-anchored – not as an abstract concept, but as part of everyday life.

ABOUT THE INITIATIVE “EHRENTAG“

On 23 May 2026, the initiative “Ehrentag” will take place for the first time. It is a nationwide initiative marking the anniversary of Germany’s Basic Law, initiated by Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier. The idea is simple: to celebrate the constitution, people across the country are invited to contribute a few hours of their time to help make their communities a little better. The focus is on participation, shared experience, and a sense of community. The Federal President’s Office is organising the day of action together with the German Foundation for Engagement and Volunteering (DSEE), based in Neustrelitz.

item.title: Building Bridges Across the Bosporus: 10 years of Stiftung Mercator’s Istanbul office
item.description:
In 2016, Stiftung Mercator’s liaison office in Turkey began its work. Since then, it has enabled exchange and dialogue between stakeholders from politics, academia and civil society – especially among young people – as well as supporting research projects and cultural initiatives. To date, the non-profit organisation has funded more than 100 projects with a total budget of over €50 million in and for the country. 

Istanbul/Essen, 17 April 2026 – One example of the office’s work under the leadership of Dr Jannes Tessmann is the Istanbul Policy Center – Sabancı University – Stiftung Mercator Initiative. Established in 2012, its core element is the Mercator-IPC Fellowship Programme. It enables researchers and practitioners from Germany and other European countries to collaborate with Turkish partners on topics such as political partnership, democratisation and climate policy. Fellows have included well-known figures such as Bulgarian political scientist Ivan Krastev, journalist Aslı Aydıntaşbaş, as well as politicians Ruprecht Polenz and Yanis Varoufakis.

Another key partner is the organisation Anadolu Kültür, which supports arts and culture in Turkey and beyond. Its well-known founder Osman Kavala has been imprisoned since 2017 on changing and unfounded charges – despite a ruling by the European Court of Human Rights ordering the Turkish judiciary to release him immediately.

“The office is the focus point of our long-standing work with and on Turkey – especially in challenging times,” says Dr Lars Grotewold, Chief Executive Officer of Stiftung Mercator. “It provides a space where exchange continues and connections are maintained, even when relations between Europe and Turkey are strained.”

Contributing to Europe’s stability and capacity to act 

“From the very beginning, the office has been one of our most important partners – and continues to be so,” emphasised German Consul General Dr Regine Grienberger in her speech at the anniversary celebration of the Stiftung Mercator Istanbul office. Through its outstanding work, she said, it brings together Turkish, German and other European actors from politics, academia and civil society to address shared challenges. “We look forward to continuing this close and productive cooperation in the years to come.”

“Strong and resilient relations with Turkey are crucial for Europe’s stability and capacity to act, whether through economic interdependence or the country’s role as a regional middle power,” says Dr. Jannes Tessmann, who has headed the office since 2019. “Through our work, we help to deepen and strengthen cooperation between Germany and Turkey.”

The liaison office in Istanbul is a key component of Stiftung Mercator’s Turkey portfolio within its Europe in the World programme area. This includes other funded projects such as the Centre for Applied Turkey Studies at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin and the German-Turkish Youth Bridge in Düsseldorf.

item.title: Sustainability remains a board-level responsibility – but momentum is fading
item.description:
In 73 per cent of companies, responsibility for sustainability transformation remains anchored at board or executive management level. Companies’ self-defined climate targets are largely maintained. However, the issue is noticeably losing priority and momentum. This is the finding of the fourth Sustainability Transformation Monitor (STM), published by Bertelsmann Stiftung, Stiftung Mercator, the University of Hamburg and the Peer School for Sustainable Development. 

The STM surveyed 822 companies from the real economy and the financial sector in Germany. It shows why momentum has been lost: companies perceive uncertain political conditions and a lack of market incentives as the biggest obstacles to increased transformation. 

In the public debate, sustainability is receding into the background. This is also affecting corporate attitudes. Among 59 per cent of companies in the real economy and financial sector, sustainability is becoming less of a priority internally. In the previous year, only around 14 per cent reported this trend. Large corporations and sizeable SMEs in particular feel the impact of current debates. 

The declining momentum is also reflected in the stagnation of responsibility at board and executive level, with no change compared to the previous year. The share of companies planning to anchor responsibility at this level has fallen by seven percentage points. 

Political uncertainty weakens key drivers of transformation 

The strongest drivers of sustainability transformation are “future employees”, followed by “executive management”, the “younger generation” and “competitors”. Notably, nearly all potential drivers have declined in intensity – in some cases significantly (employees: down 12 percentage points; executive management: down 7 percentage points). 

From a corporate perspective, the relevance of politics to the transformation process has changed most dramatically. In previous years, companies regarded political action as an important driver. In the STM 2026, its significance as a driver drops sharply by 31 percentage points. At the same time, uncertain political and regulatory frameworks are now increasingly perceived as a barrier (up to 30 percentage points). 

 Lack of economic incentives slows down progress 

“Without clear and reliable signals from policymakers and markets, the transformation is at risk of entering a phase of stagnation,” says Jakob Kunzlmann, sustainability expert at Bertelsmann Stiftung. “We now need a renewed focus: stronger strategic prioritisation, reliable political frameworks and market-based incentives, such as carbon pricing with predictable price pathways. This would allow environmental and social factors to become effective drivers of investment and competitiveness.” 

Where political pressure is lacking, the prospect of a “business case” – that is, measurable economic benefits resulting from sustainability transformation – could become more prominent. However, only 17 per cent of companies see a clear business case. While 43 per cent recognise financial added value from integrating environmental and social issues, the benefits so far fall short of the associated costs. This helps explain why around 70 per cent of companies report that insufficient economic incentives are slowing their transformation efforts. 

More companies are setting their own climate targets 

Nevertheless, sustainability transformation has not disappeared from corporate agendas. The share of companies and banks measuring their greenhouse gas emissions has risen to 86 per cent. In the real economy, climate targets are largely being maintained or further developed. The proportion of companies with self-defined climate targets has increased from 53 per cent to 59 per cent. In the financial sector, the figure has risen even more sharply, from 46 per cent to 65 per cent. 

“It is an important signal that more companies are measuring their emissions and adhering to climate targets. The crucial next step is to translate these targets into concrete transition pathways, with clear investment decisions, timelines and financing plans,” says Philipp Wesemann, Project Manager at Stiftung Mercator’s division for Climate-Resilient Society. 

However, there is still a lack of concrete implementation plans. Among companies with climate targets, 41 per cent state that their transition plan is still “in development”. “Data on transformation must be embedded in corporate management and in investment and financing decisions,” says Manuel Reppmann, project lead and sustainability expert at the University of Hamburg. 

Companies are well prepared for reporting – and committed beyond legal requirements 

The EU Omnibus procedure, aiming to simplify reporting requirements and narrow their scope, has in many cases led to a slowdown or temporary suspension of reporting processes. At the same time, around 59 per cent of companies that will be subject to reporting obligations from 2027 already consider themselves well or very well prepared for EU-wide requirements; only around 18 per cent feel insufficiently prepared. 

Furthermore, 75 per cent of companies that will in future be exempt from mandatory reporting state that they intend to continue publishing sustainability reports voluntarily. Just under 8 per cent plan to discontinue reporting altogether. 

Sustainability is present in corporate finance – but not gaining importance 

Sustainability remains part of financing practice, although its perceived relevance is declining. Only 30 per cent of companies and 37 per cent of banks consider sustainability important in financing discussions. In both groups, its importance has decreased (down 8 and 9 percentage points respectively). 

While both banks and companies expect sustainability to play a role in corporate finance in the future, agreement in the real economy stands at 45 per cent, compared to 79 per cent among financial institutions. However, expectations have declined on both sides. 

“Sustainability data is widely available today – yet its impact on lending decisions remains limited. Unless it is systematically integrated into risk analyses and pricing conditions, tangible transformation of incentives will not emerge. Sustainable finance must therefore evolve from a reporting instrument into a steering instrument,” says Incken Wentorp, sustainability expert at the Peer School for Sustainable Development. 

In this new phase of sustainability transformation, effective cooperation along value chains and between the real economy and the financial sector is becoming increasingly important. 

“Transformation is increasingly a coordination task between companies, banks, investors and policymakers. Many solutions only emerge through the interaction of these actors,” says Laura Marie Edinger-Schons, Chief Sustainability Officer and Professor of Sustainable Business at the University of Hamburg. 

Sustainability Transformation Monitor 

The STM 2026 comprises data from 822 companies, banks, and investors. It aims to provide evidence-based monitoring of the economy’s sustainability transformation. A particular focus lies on the interaction between the real economy and the financial sector in financing transformation. 

The STM is published annually and has now been issued for the fourth time in cooperation between Bertelsmann Stiftung, Stiftung Mercator, the University of Hamburg and the Peer School for Sustainable Development. The study is supported by a partner network of more than 30 associations and initiatives.

In 73 per cent of companies, responsibility for sustainability transformation remains anchored at board or executive management level. Companies’ self-defined climate targets are largely maintained. However, the issue is noticeably losing priority and momentum. This is the finding of the fourth Sustainability Transformation Monitor (STM), published by Bertelsmann Stiftung, Stiftung Mercator, the University of Hamburg and the Peer School for Sustainable Development. 

The STM surveyed 822 companies from the real economy and the financial sector in Germany. It shows why momentum has been lost: companies perceive uncertain political conditions and a lack of market incentives as the biggest obstacles to increased transformation. 

In the public debate, sustainability is receding into the background. This is also affecting corporate attitudes. Among 59 per cent of companies in the real economy and financial sector, sustainability is becoming less of a priority internally. In the previous year, only around 14 per cent reported this trend. Large corporations and sizeable SMEs in particular feel the impact of current debates. 

The declining momentum is also reflected in the stagnation of responsibility at board and executive level, with no change compared to the previous year. The share of companies planning to anchor responsibility at this level has fallen by seven percentage points. 

Political uncertainty weakens key drivers of transformation 

The strongest drivers of sustainability transformation are “future employees”, followed by “executive management”, the “younger generation” and “competitors”. Notably, nearly all potential drivers have declined in intensity – in some cases significantly (employees: down 12 percentage points; executive management: down 7 percentage points). 

From a corporate perspective, the relevance of politics to the transformation process has changed most dramatically. In previous years, companies regarded political action as an important driver. In the STM 2026, its significance as a driver drops sharply by 31 percentage points. At the same time, uncertain political and regulatory frameworks are now increasingly perceived as a barrier (up to 30 percentage points). 

 Lack of economic incentives slows down progress 

“Without clear and reliable signals from policymakers and markets, the transformation is at risk of entering a phase of stagnation,” says Jakob Kunzlmann, sustainability expert at Bertelsmann Stiftung. “We now need a renewed focus: stronger strategic prioritisation, reliable political frameworks and market-based incentives, such as carbon pricing with predictable price pathways. This would allow environmental and social factors to become effective drivers of investment and competitiveness.” 

Where political pressure is lacking, the prospect of a “business case” – that is, measurable economic benefits resulting from sustainability transformation – could become more prominent. However, only 17 per cent of companies see a clear business case. While 43 per cent recognise financial added value from integrating environmental and social issues, the benefits so far fall short of the associated costs. This helps explain why around 70 per cent of companies report that insufficient economic incentives are slowing their transformation efforts. 

More companies are setting their own climate targets 

Nevertheless, sustainability transformation has not disappeared from corporate agendas. The share of companies and banks measuring their greenhouse gas emissions has risen to 86 per cent. In the real economy, climate targets are largely being maintained or further developed. The proportion of companies with self-defined climate targets has increased from 53 per cent to 59 per cent. In the financial sector, the figure has risen even more sharply, from 46 per cent to 65 per cent. 

“It is an important signal that more companies are measuring their emissions and adhering to climate targets. The crucial next step is to translate these targets into concrete transition pathways, with clear investment decisions, timelines and financing plans,” says Philipp Wesemann, Project Manager at Stiftung Mercator’s division for Climate-Resilient Society. 

However, there is still a lack of concrete implementation plans. Among companies with climate targets, 41 per cent state that their transition plan is still “in development”. “Data on transformation must be embedded in corporate management and in investment and financing decisions,” says Manuel Reppmann, project lead and sustainability expert at the University of Hamburg. 

Companies are well prepared for reporting – and committed beyond legal requirements 

The EU Omnibus procedure, aiming to simplify reporting requirements and narrow their scope, has in many cases led to a slowdown or temporary suspension of reporting processes. At the same time, around 59 per cent of companies that will be subject to reporting obligations from 2027 already consider themselves well or very well prepared for EU-wide requirements; only around 18 per cent feel insufficiently prepared. 

Furthermore, 75 per cent of companies that will in future be exempt from mandatory reporting state that they intend to continue publishing sustainability reports voluntarily. Just under 8 per cent plan to discontinue reporting altogether. 

Sustainability is present in corporate finance – but not gaining importance 

Sustainability remains part of financing practice, although its perceived relevance is declining. Only 30 per cent of companies and 37 per cent of banks consider sustainability important in financing discussions. In both groups, its importance has decreased (down 8 and 9 percentage points respectively). 

While both banks and companies expect sustainability to play a role in corporate finance in the future, agreement in the real economy stands at 45 per cent, compared to 79 per cent among financial institutions. However, expectations have declined on both sides. 

“Sustainability data is widely available today – yet its impact on lending decisions remains limited. Unless it is systematically integrated into risk analyses and pricing conditions, tangible transformation of incentives will not emerge. Sustainable finance must therefore evolve from a reporting instrument into a steering instrument,” says Incken Wentorp, sustainability expert at the Peer School for Sustainable Development. 

In this new phase of sustainability transformation, effective cooperation along value chains and between the real economy and the financial sector is becoming increasingly important. 

“Transformation is increasingly a coordination task between companies, banks, investors and policymakers. Many solutions only emerge through the interaction of these actors,” says Laura Marie Edinger-Schons, Chief Sustainability Officer and Professor of Sustainable Business at the University of Hamburg. 

Sustainability Transformation Monitor 

The STM 2026 comprises data from 822 companies, banks, and investors. It aims to provide evidence-based monitoring of the economy’s sustainability transformation. A particular focus lies on the interaction between the real economy and the financial sector in financing transformation. 

The STM is published annually and has now been issued for the fourth time in cooperation between Bertelsmann Stiftung, Stiftung Mercator, the University of Hamburg and the Peer School for Sustainable Development. The study is supported by a partner network of more than 30 associations and initiatives.

item.title: New Think Tank for Financing the Economic Transition
item.description:
Stiftung Mercator has established Finance for Transition – Centre for Resilient Economy and Finance, a Berlin-based think tank designed to show how private capital can be strategically mobilized for the modernization and decarbonization of the economy. The centre will be led by Silke Stremlau, one of the most prominent voices in Germany’s sustainable finance market. 

Geopolitical conflicts, extreme weather events, and technological disruptions are putting pressure on the economy. This calls for far-reaching modernization of companies – an effort that often fails due to a lack of investment incentives and insufficient coordination between politics, business, and financial markets. Finance for Transition (F4T for short) addresses this challenge by combining academic expertise with practical implementation. 

“Despite the many established instruments, access to capital remains a key bottleneck when it comes to improving competitiveness through sustainable business models – especially for small and medium-sized enterprises,” says Dr. Lars Grotewold, Chief Executive Officer of Stiftung Mercator, describing a central economic policy challenge to which F4T will contribute solutions. The new think-and-do tank will therefore systematically identify the structural barriers that hinder the mobilization of private capital on the part of companies and investors. In the initial funding phase, Stiftung Mercator will provide €7.1 million over five years. 

Solutions for the Heat Transition in Municipalities 

“To remove these obstacles, we bring together financial markets, companies, policymakers, academia, and civil society,” explains Silke Stremlau, Managing Director of F4T. “We will translate between worlds and build bridges.” She gained experience with this approach during the previous legislative period as Chair of the German Federal Government’s Sustainable Finance Advisory Council. In addition, she led the pension fund Hannoversche Kassen, served as an authorized officer at Bank in Bistum Essen, and was a partner at imug Consulting. 

Stremlau and her team will consolidate and apply existing knowledge on transition finance to advance the decarbonization of the economy. F4T will also develop practical, pre-competitive solutions – for example in the area of the municipal heat transition. At present, many municipal utilities face a challenge: local savings banks or cooperative banks are often unable to provide loans of the required scale, while for large institutional investors the projects are too small. One possible approach is to bundle projects involving several municipal utilities – an option that, however, entails regulatory and organizational challenges. New forms of cooperation are needed to address these issues.

item.title: Start of the New Five-Year Strategy Period
item.description:
Balancing continuity and change, the charitable Stiftung Mercator has updated the strategy that will guide its work over the next five years. At the same time, Lars Grotewold assumed his new role as Chairman of the Executive Board at the beginning of the year, succeeding Wolfgang Rohe, who is stepping down due to his retirement.

Stiftung Mercator will continue to focus its work on digitalisation, Europe’s role in the world, climate, and participation and social cohesion. At the same time, it has further refined its goals and approaches across all program areas. For example, the former Climate Action Centre will broaden its scope to explicitly include adaptation to the growing impacts of climate change. The aim is to advance an integrated and socially just climate policy that brings together effective mitigation, the active removal of greenhouse gases from the atmosphere, and strengthened resilience to climate impacts. Reflecting this evolution, the Centre has been given the new name Climate-Resilient Society.

“Throughout the new strategic period, we will continue to adapt our work whenever this is required by an environment marked by uncertainty and multiple, overlapping crises,” said Lars Grotewold, the foundation’s new Chairman of the Executive Board , who previously led the Climate Action Centre. “This requires organisational agility, a willingness to take informed risks, and systematic, cross-program learning”.

Joining forces with democratic groups

Within the Participation and Cohesion Centre, priorities have also shifted. The focus is now even more strongly on socioeconomically disadvantaged people, regardless of their background, and on promoting fair access to opportunities – for example in the labour market and housing sector. To strengthen trust in public institutions and the liberal democratic order, the Centre supports democratic structures, particularly at the local level.

The Digital Society Centre supports initiatives aimed at advancing the digital transformation of the state to enhance its capacity to act in the public interest. It also works to curb platform business models that undermine democratic processes. In addition, the Centre seeks to better connect digital policy with other thematic fields and broader societal debates.

Against the backdrop of a rapidly changing global order – and particularly a reassessment of transatlantic relations – the Europe in the World Centre promotes exchange among academia, civil society, politics, and business to help shape a renewed European self-understanding. This approach combines internal cohesion with a more strategic engagement in external relations. One key area of work is access to critical raw materials. The foundation’s focus countries, China and Turkey, where Stiftung Mercator maintains its own offices, play an important role in this context.

“Our overarching ambition remains to enable social progress that serves the common good,” Grotewold emphasized. “This is something we can only achieve in close collaboration with a broad alliance of democratic actors.”

Stiftung Mercator / Peter Gwiazda

About Lars Grotewold
Dr. Lars Grotewold has been Chairman of the Executive Board of Stiftung Mercator since January 1, 2026. He previously built and led the foundation’s Climate Action division starting in 2009. In this role, he was responsible for the strategic development of the funding portfolio and partner network. He is a co-founder of several leading policy think tanks, including Agora Energiewende, Agora Verkehrswende, the Mercator Research Institute on Global Commons and Climate Change, and the energy and climate news service Clean Energy Wire. Before joining Stiftung Mercator, the PhD-trained molecular biologist worked at the secretariat of the German Council of Science and Humanities (Wissenschaftsrat) following research appointments in Germany and abroad.

item.title: Klaus Scharioth: Mentor, Humanitarian and Diplomat has Passed Away
item.description:
The Mercator Fellowship on International Affairs, Stiftung Mercator, the German Academic Scholarship Foundation and the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke mourn the loss of Dr Klaus Scharioth. He passed away on 30 October 2025 at the age of 79. After 35 years in Foreign Service, most recently as German Ambassador to the United States, he served as Rector of the Mercator Fellowship from 2011 to 2024, leaving a lasting mark on the institution. Until his death, he was also Chairman of the Advisory Board of the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke, whose development he had supported with his advice and as a door opener since 2013.

As rector of the Mercator Fellowship on International Affairs, Klaus Scharioth supported generations of fellows “who want to make a difference and gave them the tools they need to do so,” as he himself put it. He prepared them, with passion and conviction, to work for a better world. He always encouraged the fellows to express critical views clearly yet kindly, always urging open dialogue, behind closed doors, in the spirit of his personal motto: “Don’t be afraid of royal thrones.” He loved discussing the fellows’ questions on long walks with them, genuinely engaging with their ideas and often remarking that he learned just as much from them. He called his work for the Mercator Fellowship a “stroke of luck for me”.

“Klaus Scharioth has made an invaluable contribution to the Mercator Fellowship and to the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke. Without him, neither institution would be what it is today,” says Dr Wolfgang Rohe, Chairman of the Executive Board of the Stiftung Mercator, in recognition of his achievements. “He was a masterful questioner in conversations, and those who answered his questions always came away with a better and more precise understanding of their own point of view.” With unwavering energy and great confidence, he opened doors and connected people and institutions. His passion was to nurture young talent and support them on their journey. The many alumni of the Fellowship will always remain grateful to him.

Dr Annette Julius, Secretary General of the German Academic Scholarship Foundation, adds: “Klaus Scharioth embodied an extremely rare combination of broad international experience, the highest level of professional competence and authority, and at the same time remarkable approachability, attentiveness, and humility. Supporting the fellows was not a mere duty to him, but a matter close to his heart.” His unique ability to listen, to engage with people on an equal footing, and to challenge them to self-reflect with precise questions created encounters of true depth and mutual respect.

“Klaus Scharioth impressed us all with his unwavering commitment to mutual understanding and his sincere interest in the people he met.” Dr Daniel Grütjen, Managing Director of the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke explains. “He asked questions and listened attentively instead of putting himself in the spotlight. It was a privilege to work alongside him and learn from him.” Scharioth had chaired the organisation’s Advisory Board since 2013, guiding it through difficult discussions with integrity, clarity and professionalism. His humanity and his deep conviction of the importance of German-Turkish youth exchange were a constant inspiration and a moral compass for our team.

Our thoughts are with his family. Klaus Scharioth was married and father of three children. We will remember him with great gratitude: as a role model, an inspiration and a lasting commitment to our work.

About Klaus Scharioth
Dr Klaus Scharioth served as Rector of the Mercator Fellowship on International Affairs from 2011 to 2024 and chaired the Advisory Board of the German-Turkish Youth Bridge from 2013 onwards. From 2006 to 2011, he was Germany’s Ambassador to the United States. Prior to that, he held the post of State Secretary at the Federal Foreign Office (2002–2006). Having joined the diplomatic service in 1976, Scharioth held numerous senior positions, including Political Director at the Federal Foreign Office and at NATO. Most recently, he taught at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy in Medford, Massachusetts, where he also earned his doctorate following studies in law and related disciplines.

The Mercator Fellowship on International Affairs, Stiftung Mercator, the German Academic Scholarship Foundation and the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke mourn the loss of Dr Klaus Scharioth. He passed away on 30 October 2025 at the age of 79. After 35 years in Foreign Service, most recently as German Ambassador to the United States, he served as Rector of the Mercator Fellowship from 2011 to 2024, leaving a lasting mark on the institution. Until his death, he was also Chairman of the Advisory Board of the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke, whose development he had supported with his advice and as a door opener since 2013.

As rector of the Mercator Fellowship on International Affairs, Klaus Scharioth supported generations of fellows “who want to make a difference and gave them the tools they need to do so,” as he himself put it. He prepared them, with passion and conviction, to work for a better world. He always encouraged the fellows to express critical views clearly yet kindly, always urging open dialogue, behind closed doors, in the spirit of his personal motto: “Don’t be afraid of royal thrones.” He loved discussing the fellows’ questions on long walks with them, genuinely engaging with their ideas and often remarking that he learned just as much from them. He called his work for the Mercator Fellowship a “stroke of luck for me”.

“Klaus Scharioth has made an invaluable contribution to the Mercator Fellowship and to the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke. Without him, neither institution would be what it is today,” says Dr Wolfgang Rohe, Chairman of the Executive Board of the Stiftung Mercator, in recognition of his achievements. “He was a masterful questioner in conversations, and those who answered his questions always came away with a better and more precise understanding of their own point of view.” With unwavering energy and great confidence, he opened doors and connected people and institutions. His passion was to nurture young talent and support them on their journey. The many alumni of the Fellowship will always remain grateful to him.

Dr Annette Julius, Secretary General of the German Academic Scholarship Foundation, adds: “Klaus Scharioth embodied an extremely rare combination of broad international experience, the highest level of professional competence and authority, and at the same time remarkable approachability, attentiveness, and humility. Supporting the fellows was not a mere duty to him, but a matter close to his heart.” His unique ability to listen, to engage with people on an equal footing, and to challenge them to self-reflect with precise questions created encounters of true depth and mutual respect.

“Klaus Scharioth impressed us all with his unwavering commitment to mutual understanding and his sincere interest in the people he met.” Dr Daniel Grütjen, Managing Director of the Deutsch-Türkische Jugendbrücke explains. “He asked questions and listened attentively instead of putting himself in the spotlight. It was a privilege to work alongside him and learn from him.” Scharioth had chaired the organisation’s Advisory Board since 2013, guiding it through difficult discussions with integrity, clarity and professionalism. His humanity and his deep conviction of the importance of German-Turkish youth exchange were a constant inspiration and a moral compass for our team.

Our thoughts are with his family. Klaus Scharioth was married and father of three children. We will remember him with great gratitude: as a role model, an inspiration and a lasting commitment to our work.

About Klaus Scharioth
Dr Klaus Scharioth served as Rector of the Mercator Fellowship on International Affairs from 2011 to 2024 and chaired the Advisory Board of the German-Turkish Youth Bridge from 2013 onwards. From 2006 to 2011, he was Germany’s Ambassador to the United States. Prior to that, he held the post of State Secretary at the Federal Foreign Office (2002–2006). Having joined the diplomatic service in 1976, Scharioth held numerous senior positions, including Political Director at the Federal Foreign Office and at NATO. Most recently, he taught at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy in Medford, Massachusetts, where he also earned his doctorate following studies in law and related disciplines.

item.title: Committed to a Resilient Democracy and Society: Stiftung Mercator supported over 100 projects in 2024
item.description:
In 2024, Stiftung Mercator approved 108 new projects with a total funding volume of over 58 million euros. The foundation focused its support on initiatives in the fields of Digital Society, Europe in the World, Climate Action, and Participation and Cohesion. It also transitioned two of its long-standing partner organisations into independence, as outlined in its annual report published today. 

In response to growing public mistrust in democratic institutions, Stiftung Mercator continues to support projects that foster participation and drive forward the social and sustainable transformation of society. “In times of overlapping national and international crises, strong alliances and a genuine willingness to change are more important than ever,” says Dr Wolfgang Rohe, Chairman of the Executive Board. “Only together can we move from analysing problems to implementing real solutions.” 

Among the newly launched projects is the non-partisan Initiative for an Effective State (Initiative für einen handlungsfähigen Staat), which Stiftung Mercator has supported since the end of 2024 – according to its motto #StandingUpForDemocracy. The initiative puts forward proposals for reforming the state and public administration. It is one of 108 newly approved projects with a total budget of over 58 million euros that the organisation launched last year. 

Projects advancing Rule of Law and Digital Sovereignty 

Other examples include support for Aktion Zivilcourage, which offers local moderation training in Eastern Germany to manage crisis and conflict situations – strengthening civic engagement in the face of right-wing extremism and anti-democratic forces. Meanwhile, partners like Rule of Law Clinic are analysing how effectively the EU enforces its own rule-of-law standards and protects fundamental rights. 

The foundation has also set new priorities in the area of socially just climate action. One example is its support for a monitoring study by International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), which explores ways to expand access to electric mobility for low-income groups. The widespread use of disinformation and propaganda through digital channels – especially during 2024’s super election year – was another key focus. Through a diverse funding portfolio, Stiftung Mercator continues to promote greater digital sovereignty across Europe.

At the end of 2024, two key partners reached a major milestone: Ruhr University Bochum, TU Dortmund University, and the University of Duisburg-Essen are continuing the work of the Mercator Research Centre Ruhr (MERCUR) – founded 15 years ago – now with their own resources. In addition, the Mercator Research Institute on Global Commons and Climate Change (MCC) has become part of the renowned Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) as its fifth research department. 

Since its founding, Stiftung Mercator has supported 2,160 projects with a total of 1.02 billion euros (as of the end of 2024). Funding primarily supports research institutions, civil society organisations, and think tanks, typically over multi-year periods.

item.title: Initiative presents final report on state reform
item.description:
The Initiative for an Effective State presented its final report to Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier today. With the coalition agreement of the current federal government incorporating numerous key recommendations, the four initiators of the initiative are urging that these reforms be pursued as a “major collective endeavor”. The report also offers further recommendations, including the need for political parties to renew themselves to remain relevant; the potential of model municipalities and regions to pilot new reform approaches and drive implementation; and the growing influence of social media as a threat to democracy: “this issue must be placed at the top of the political agenda”.

With a call to the CDU/CSU-SPD governing coalition and the federal states for decisive action, the Initiative for an Effective State concludes its work. “The will to change this country and pursue state reform runs through the coalition agreement,” states the final report. Many of the initiative’s recommendations are reflected in it. Now the focus must be on implementation: “If even half of these plans were realised, this country would be a different one.” The final report and further information can be found on the initiative’s website: Initiative for an Effective State.

On Monday, the four initiators Julia Jäkel, Thomas de Maizière, Peer Steinbrück, and Andreas Voßkuhle presented their final report to Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the initiative’s patron. The report revisits the discussion around their recommendations since the interim report in March and evaluates the coalition agreement in light of those proposals. It also expands the report from 30 to 35 recommendations.

To implement the plans in the coalition agreement, state reform must be seen as a shared responsibility, the initiators emphasise. A single Minister for Digital Affairs and State Modernisation is not enough: “Silo thinking must now be set aside.” The Chancellor and Vice-Chancellor must drive reforms forward, with federal and state governments pulling in the same direction. As a “solid and binding foundation,” the initiators highlight the joint modernisation agenda adopted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the state premiers on 18 June 2025.

Across politics and administration, reforms require a critical mass: “Those committed to renewal from within must be empowered, and doers from outside must be attracted,” the report says.

The initiative also sees political parties as having a duty to renew themselves. The success of state reform “centrally depends on the parties’ internal capacity to reform.” Action is needed: parties are losing credibility, and “internal decision-making risks losing touch with real life.”

To accelerate the implementation of reforms in public administration, the initiators recommend the creation of model municipalities and model regions, where proposals for modernising the entire administration can be tested. These could trial simplified application and approval procedures, faster citizen services, and a new culture around personnel, leadership, and dealing with errors. Among those actively volunteering for this are the city of Stralsund (Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) and the Cologne administrative district.

Another key to an effective state is countering the threat to democracy posed by social media. These platforms have acquired significant political power: “But the exercise of power requires control and order.” Proposed measures include the elimination of liability exemptions for social media platforms regarding the content they distribute and stricter enforcement of youth protection laws. “This issue,” the initiators stress, “belongs at the top of the political agenda!”

The final report also includes new recommendations for the work of intelligence services, which are “too dependent on intelligence from allied services.” They should be given comparable powers to other services for foreign intelligence.

The initiators also make proposals for skilled labour immigration. Access to the labour market should be expedited, and integration made easier through a ‘One Shop’ process involving coordination between relevant authorities.

The Initiative for an Effective State ends its work with the publication of the final report: “We wanted to provide an impetus for state reform – we consider that goal achieved. We can and do not want to be a permanent oversight or advisory body.”

This reform project is a joint initiative of media executive and supervisory board member Julia Jäkel, former federal ministers Thomas de Maizière and Peer Steinbrück, and constitutional law scholar and long-time President of the Federal Constitutional Court Andreas Voßkuhle. Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier served as patron. The initiators acted voluntarily, independently of political parties or interest groups, and aimed to “help overcome blockages and self-blockages in government action.”

The initiative is financially and organisationally supported by four prominent foundations: the Hertie Foundation, the Fritz Thyssen Foundation, the Mercator Foundation, and the ZEIT Stiftung Bucerius. The Hertie School in Berlin served as the initiative’s Head Office.

To develop their recommendations, the four initiators worked with 54 experts in seven working groups. Participants came from various fields and regions of Germany – including mayors, school principals, entrepreneurs, public administration professionals, researchers and IT specialists. The report also incorporates feedback from numerous alumni of the supporting foundations, young professionals from business, science, and administration.

The report will be published as a book on 12 August by Herder Verlag and will be available online from 11:00 AM at Initiative for an Effective State | Hertie School.
